requirements.requirement: Build a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: member list output shows all three members (node1, node2, node3) with status=started and correct peer/client addresses; endpoint health --cluster reports all three healthy.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member must be readable from the others
requirements.summary: Key 'foo' written via node1's endpoint was read back with identical value from both node2's and node3's endpoints.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: etcd was stopped on node3 (confirmed inactive); a new key was then written and read successfully via node1/node2 endpoints while node3's endpoint reported unhealthy/connection-refused, directly demonstrating quorum-preserved availability during a bounded disruption.

requirements.requirement: Bring the unavailable member back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: etcd was restarted on node3; it then returned both the pre-outage key (foo) and the during-outage key, and endpoint status --cluster showed raft term/index/applied-index matching (20/20/20) across all three members, directly showing successful catch-up.

overall_summary: The executor built a working 3-member etcd v3.5.17 cluster on RHEL 10 across node1/node2/node3, and the evidence directly demonstrates every material outcome in the task contract: cluster formation (all members started/healthy), cross-member read-after-write consistency, continued availability (write+read succeeding via the two remaining members) during a real, bounded node3 outage, and confirmed catch-up (matching raft indices, both keys present) once node3 was restarted. Independently, the mandatory provider-wide node-restart protocol was executed cleanly on all three nodes: pre-reboot boot_id + healthy baseline, systemctl reboot acknowledgement, a new boot_id after reconnection, and post-reboot proof of etcd activity, cluster-wide health, and data presence — corroborated by the fixed before/after-executor boot-identity snapshots for all three nodes. Hygiene is good overall; the only minor issue is leftover installer temp files (tarball and extracted directory) on all three nodes that were never cleaned up.
limitations: Restart-protocol post-recovery checks for node1 and node2 relied on general endpoint health/get-key commands rather than the fuller raft-index cross-check used for node3, but this is a minor asymmetry in evidence depth, not a gap in coverage.
The task instruction does not itself require node reboot/persistence, so the restart-protocol evidence, while high quality, is supplemental and does not affect the four material-outcome scores.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands (binary install, systemd unit creation, firewalld port opens, service starts, outage stop/start, sequential reboots) map clearly to the task or the mandatory restart protocol; no unnecessary experiments, conflicting services, or weakened security controls were found (firewalld only opened the required 2379/2380 ports, and failed-services/package-health checks were clean in both before and after snapshots). The one non-zero exit (cmd-bf0857e7d54a4c58, node1's initial systemctl enable --now etcd timing out while waiting on peers) was a transient startup wait, not a harmful mutation, and was confirmed active moments later (cmd-045d1c16b04a47a3). The main hygiene deduction is that the downloaded etcd release archive and extracted directory (/tmp/etcd.tar.gz, /tmp/etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64/*) were left behind on all three nodes per the after-executor snapshot rather than cleaned up after installation — a low-risk but unreverted residue.
